sections.html:
Lafayette is the Tippecanoe County seat, on the southeast bank of the Wabash River across from West Lafayette, about 63 miles northwest of Indianapolis. The 2020 census counted 70,783 residents, and the housing stock is mostly built out rather than spreading fast. Older streets run downhill toward the river, newer subdivisions sit on the plateau and the outer edges, and Purdue University across the bridge pulls renters and investors into the same market as long-time owners.

Manufacturing and Purdue drive the job market, with employers such as Wabash National and Subaru of Indiana Automotive. Demand for housing follows plant shifts and the academic calendar, and a job change or transfer out of town is one of the most common reasons owners here want a quick sale.

Lafayette was platted in 1825, and the age and condition of a house usually follow the neighborhood. Historic districts include Ninth Street Hill and Upper Main Street, plus Downtown, Ellsworth, Highland Park, Jefferson, Perrin and St. Mary's. Outer neighborhoods such as Vinton Highlands and Jesco Hills Estates were developed later.

Houses in the historic neighborhoods carry the repair needs that come with age, and that is a common reason an owner decides repairs are not worth chasing before a sale. If your house is inside a historic district, check with the city before you plan exterior work. A buyer who purchases as-is takes that question over.

Lafayette has cold winters and warm, humid summers, with an average January low of 17.7 degrees F, an average July high of 83.6 degrees F and about 20.5 inches of snow a year. Freeze and thaw cycles are hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys and driveways, and heating costs matter in the old housing stock.

The Wabash is the other factor. USGS flood inundation maps cover about 4.8 miles of the river at Lafayette and show how far water spreads at each river stage. If your house is near the river, look up the flood zone, because a buyer's lender and insurer will ask the same question.

sections.h2: Fix it first or sell as-is?
sections.html: Walk through the house the way a buyer's inspector would. Note the roof, gutters, chimney, foundation, plumbing and heating system, which take the most punishment from Lafayette winters. Get rough quotes for each item, then add the weeks the work will take. A buyer with a mortgage typically comes back after inspection with a repair request or a lower offer. A cash buyer prices the condition at the start. If repairs would use up most of what they add, an as-is sale may net about the same money with far less effort.

OfficeLocationHours
County RecorderCounty Office Building, 2nd floor, 20 North 3rd StreetMonday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
County Treasurer20 N 3rd Street, 2nd Floor, LafayetteWeekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The city generally requires permits for property modifications. Routine maintenance, non-structural reroofing and landscaping are exempt.

  • A shed on a permanent foundation, or over 120 square feet, needs a building permit and must meet setbacks.
  • Fences do not need a permit, but residential fences in a street frontage setback are capped at 42 inches.
  • Short-term rentals fall under Ordinance 2017-27, and a $100 application fee was set by Ordinance 2018-01 for the transient rental registration permit.
  • The city does not survey property lines, so a surveyor is the answer to boundary doubts.

Owners of dead trees on private land are responsible for them. Tell any buyer about unpermitted work.

Before the Recorder will file a deed, it has to pass through the County Assessor and the Auditor, and the Assessor wants a sales disclosure form first. Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3 has the parties complete that form before the document reaches the auditor, with the assessor approving it. A single form can cover contiguous parcels in one taxing district on a single deed.

At closing, a title or escrow company usually takes care of every step.

Lafayette owners pay property tax in a spring installment on May 10 and a fall installment on November 10. A payment mailed to the Treasurer must carry a federal postmark by the deadline, since meter dates are not accepted.

Selling mid-year? Ask the closing agent how taxes will be split between you and the buyer, so the settlement statement holds no surprises. Tax owed at closing is paid from your proceeds.

Lafayette School Corporation serves most of the city and runs Jefferson High School. Tippecanoe School Corporation serves outlying areas and operates McCutcheon High School and William Henry Harrison High School. Which district a house falls into depends on the address, so confirm with the district rather than assuming from the mailing city.

sections.h2: Steps from first call to closing
sections.html:
1. Send the address and describe the house, any tenants and any known problems.
  2. We look at the property and give you an offer.
  3. If you accept, the title company opens the file and searches for liens and unpaid taxes.
  4. You sign the deed paperwork and the sales disclosure form.
  5. The deed passes through the Assessor and Auditor, the Recorder files it, and you receive your proceeds.

Most delays come from title questions: an old lien, a name on the deed that was never updated or probate papers still outstanding. Raise them on the first call.

Owners here most often sell because of inherited homes, tenant problems, out-of-town moves, deferred repairs or mounting payments. An older house in a historic neighborhood may need foundation, plumbing and roof work that costs more than a listing would recover.

  • Listing with an agent means preparing, showing and waiting on a buyer's financing and inspection.
  • Selling yourself saves the commission but puts marketing and paperwork on you.
  • A cash buyer purchases the house as it is, and you pick the closing date.

Compare each option on net proceeds and timing, not the headline number alone.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
We buy Lafayette houses as-is. Tell us about the house and we make an offer. If you accept, a title company searches the deed, prepares the disclosure form and sets the closing date you chose. Since no lender must approve a mortgage, timing follows the title work. You need not repair, clean or stage, though disclosing known problems keeps the sale clean.

Have your tax bill, any lease and mortgage payoff figures ready for the first call. Ask for the closing date in writing.

An inherited Lafayette house may need probate before a deed can be prepared, and it may need a clean-out. Heirs who live out of town often carry utilities, insurance and property tax on an empty house. Collect the estate papers, the tax bill and the keys, and ask the title company what the deed needs.

A rental sold with a tenant keeps its lease. Gather the lease and tell any buyer the rent, deposit and term, and mention any short-term rental registration.

faqs.q: Do I need to repair my Lafayette house before selling for cash?
faqs.a: No. A cash buyer purchases the house in its current condition, so repairs, cleaning and staging are not required. You can still disclose known problems, which keeps the sale clean.

faqs.q: Which county is Lafayette in, and who records the deed?
faqs.a: Lafayette is in Tippecanoe County. The Tippecanoe County Recorder, at 20 North 3rd Street, records deeds after the Assessor and Auditor process the sales disclosure form.

faqs.q: When are Tippecanoe County property taxes due?
faqs.a: May 10 and November 10. Mailed payments must be federally postmarked by the deadline.

faqs.q: Does Lafayette require a permit for short-term rentals?
faqs.a: Yes. Short-term rentals are regulated under city Ordinance 2017-27, and a $100 application fee was set for a transient rental registration permit. Check with the city for current details.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lafayette house that sits near the Wabash River?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer or lender may check the flood zone, and USGS flood inundation maps cover about 4.8 miles of the river at Lafayette. A cash buyer can still purchase the house as-is.
